title: Michigan Republican Tom Barrett Is Now Sour On Trump’s War in Iran—But Still Took Plenty of Defense Cash
author: Julian Andreone

While Republican Rep. Tom Barrett has been actively working to distance
himself from President Donald Trump and the administration's unpopular war in
Iran, defense industry PACs and executives have poured more than $58,000 into
Republican Rep. Tom Barrett's bid for reelection in Michigan's 7th district.
He has also been on the happy end of at least a million dollars in super PAC
support from Trump.

Barrett broke with Trump over the Iran war in May after he repeatedly voted to
support the war. In April, [he cast a tie-breaking
vote](https://clerk.house.gov/evs/2026/roll114.xml) to defeat a war powers
resolution aimed at ending it. The measure failed 214-213.

Of the nearly $60,000 Barrett has received directly from the defense industry,
$38,000 has come from defense contractors like Oracle, Lockheed Martin, Booz
Allen Hamilton and General Dynamics. The congressman notably received $10,000
from Oshkosh Corporation, a military vehicles and systems manufacturer, and
$7,000 from SpaceX, Elon Musk's aerospace giant, which provides the Department
of War with missile tracking and launch services and satellite communications.

But Barrett, set to face off against Democratic challenger Will Lawrence in
November, has also received significant donations from defense industry CEOs
individually. Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar donated $7,000 to the Republican
incumbent's campaign, while Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey donated $5,500 and
General Atomics CEO Neal Blue chipped in a humble $4,996 of his own fortune.

The financial support from corporations profiting massively throughout the
Iran War has not stopped the congressman from switching to vote in favor of
Iran WPRs, joining Democrats and a few Republicans on all four introduced
since the middle of May.

Barrett has also made a concerted rhetorical attempt as of late to highlight
distance between his purported position on the war and the president's. He has
said, for instance, that the U.S. "cannot be dragged into another endless war"
and that, "There's a growing number of members that are having concerns about
the growing nature of this without any congressional authorization." He has
also called for "clearly defined" missions and end dates for the conflict.

Nevertheless, Barrett accepted defense industry contributions as recently as
the last week of June, after a number of these comments were made and votes
were cast.

Approached for comment on whether Barrett's relationship with defense
contractors and industry executives could inhibit his ability to materially
oppose the Iran War in the next Congress, a spokesperson dismissed the premise
out of hand.

"One has nothing to do with the other," Jason Roe, a Barrett spokesperson,
said.
